label: paragraph_title
text: BRITAIN'S VAST CREDIT.

label: text
text: ANSWER TO CRITICS.

label: text
text: The Chancellor of the Exchequer in the House of Commons yesterday refuted charges by the Labour Party that the return to gold is in any sense a gamble.

label: paragraph_title
text: GOLD BAR SALES.

label: paragraph_title
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text: In the House of Commons, the Financial Secretary of the Treasury, Lieutenant-Colonel W. Guinness, moving the second reading of the Gold Standard Bill pointed out in connection with the proposal that the Bank of England was bound to sell gold in amounts of not less than 400 eunecs troy fine gold in bar, that

label: paragraph_title
text: CREDIT FOR BRITAIN

label: vision_footnote

label: text
text: each bar should be worth about $1,700, and the size of the bar alone would prevent this proposal being used to bring back gold into general use and limit the possible drawing of gold for export.

label: text
text: The clause of the Bill empowering the Treasury to borrow for exchange operations had not increased the total money to be borrowed. Any sums raised under these powers must come out of the usual provision for borrowing up to the total of the supply services for the year voted yearly in the Appropriation Act. Two credits had already been conditionally negotiated under this.

label: text
text: L.L. Col. Guinness said that credit had been arranged with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York who had undertaken to give the Bank of England a revolving credit of $200,000,000 for two years from May 10.

label: text
text: The second arrangement was with the syndicate beaded by Messrs. J. P. Morgan to His

label: text

Lt. Col Guinness hoped that in view of the urgency of the matter the House would pass the measure without delay. He did not fear a rise in the bank rate or higher prices.

label: text
text: The Government believed we had reached the stage of the purchasing power being at parity, and that in the long run the producer would have more gain from the security of the gold standard than the banking interest.

label: paragraph_title
text: Labour's Protest.

label: text
text: Mr. Philip Snowden, Chancellor of the Exchequer in the Labour Cabinet, moved a Labour amendment refusing to assent to the bill, which he said by providing for return to the gold standard

label: text
text: with undue precipitancy might aggravate the existing grave conditions of unemployment and trade depression.

label: text
text: Mr. Snowden emphasised that he did not oppose the return to the gold standard, but he protested against the Government's precipitancy.

label: text
text: The Labour Party, he said; by the amendment dissociated themselves from the disastrous consequences which might result. (Ministerial laughter.)

Mr. Snowden said he did not accept Mr. Churchill's statement of the existence of a practical parity between prices in Britain and the United States. He, Mr. Snowden, thought that the difference amounted to five per cent. The Government should have united a little longer in the hope that parity of the gold level and prices could be reached by the formal operation of trade.

label: paragraph_title
text: Finest Expert Advice.

label: text
text: Mr. Winston Churchill, Chancellor of the Exchequer, denied that the decision was characterised by precipitancy. On the contrary, he said, they had secured the finest expert financial advice in the world. The Government had taken every precaution which forethought, patience and long preparation could suggest.

label: text
text: He mentioned the disadvantage of giving long notice of the return to gold and pointed out that if we had waited for the Act to expire at the end of the year everyone could under the existing law have withdrawn and hoarded gold against the date of free export, namely January, when the normal demand for bullion is high. He insisted that no country in the world was less able to afford diverging from economic facts than Britain. As regards the allegation that the decision would shackle them to America, the Chancellor said it would certainly shackle them to reality for good or ill. He personally believed it was the only basis offering permanent security.

label: paragraph_title
text: Our Vast Credit.

label: text
text: Mr. Churchill knew of nothing which would justify as increase in the rate in the immediate future. Indeed the situation was stable and, everything tended to show that the transition to gold up to the present had been effected—he was not going to prophesy about the future—with great success.

label: text
text: Mr. Churchill declared that Britain was not only the financial centre of the world, she was the centre of a wide Empire. If we detached ourselves from their movements we ran a great risk of becoming isolated and loosening the bond, whereas the fortification thereof was indispensable to our well being.

label: text
text: Mr. Churchill scouted the suggestion we might be unable to hold our own against strong trans-Atlantic influences.

label: text
text: He poinied out that Britain still controlled a vast amount of the world's business and had magnificent credits, also £3,000,000,000 in foreign investments.

label: text
text: She held £153,000,000 in gold and the Dominions held £107,000,-000. The Empire supplied seventy per cent. of the world's gold.

label: text
text: An Enormous Power.

label: text
text: The House of Commons passed the second reading of the Gold Standard Bill without division.

label: text
text: Mr. Churchm cited instances of pre-war discrepancies in the British and American price levels and their normal timely readjustment in order to disprove that absolute equation of prices was essential to the restoration of the gold standard.

label: text
text: Mr. Churchill concluded by saying that the Dominions united were an enormous power. They were great, intricate and comprehensive enough to exist side by side in amicable association with an even larger economic financial power without their own essential independence being prejudicially affected.

label: paragraph_title
text: GREAT WELCOME.

label: paragraph_title
text: HAILED BY STUDENTS.

label: text
text: (Reuter's Scrolloe.)

label: paragraph_title
text: Capetown, May 1.

label: text
text: The Prince of Wales motored to the Nationalist stronghold of Stellenbosch. He was welcomed enthusiastically, twenty-four stalwart young Dutch students hauling him in an open carriage a distance of two miles to the sports ground, where he addressed the assembled students of the local university.

label: vision_footnote

label: text
text: The Prince lunched at the agricultural Hall and afterwards notored to Huguenot Station where he joined the Royal train in which he makes his long trek.

label: paragraph_title
text: Earlier Cables.

label: paragraph_title
text: (Keuter's Service.)

label: text
text: At the dinner to the Prince of Wales, the Premier, General Hertzog was warmly applauded for his speech supporting the toast to His Royal Highness. He said the Prince would be welcomed equally and sincerely on the lovely plains of the Free State, and the high veldt of the Transvaal.

label: text
text: General Smuts said the South Africans loved the Prince's simplicity, human ways and sincerity. The people were deeply attached to him as heir apparent to the throne.

label: paragraph_title
text: TIED HANDS.

label: text
text: BELGIUES POLITICAL

label: text
text: It is feared that deadlock which aided the balance of the Parties and deprived the country of a government for the past month can only be solved by another general election.

label: text
text: Since the Socialists have declared to form a homogeneous ministry, the Catholic Right has decided to form a bloc with the Conservatives and Christian Democrats, but a section of the Relds who could support either the Catholics or Socialists are determined not to share the responsibility of government while the Catholic clubs vehemently oppose a combination of Catholics and Socialists.

label: text
text: Fence all the parties have tied hands and the crisis is only soluble, part from fresh elections, by a cabinet composed of non-members of Parliament.

SHOTS IN A POLLING BOOTH.
TWO PEOPLE KILLED.

label: paragraph_title
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text: The final results of the municipal elections are not expected until to-night at the earliest, but the fact emerges that the Left Cartel have gained advantages while the Communist have had severe setbacks.

label: text
text: Second polls are necessary in a number of cases.

label: text
text: The only disturbing incident occurred in Corsica, where shots were fired inside a polling station. Two people were killed and three injured.

label: text
text: The 'Swarajist' outlook was surveyed by the leader, Mr. C. R. Das, in his presidential address before the Bengal Provincial Congress at Faridpur. Mr. Das said Swaraj was attainable within the British Empire because the Dominion status expresses and implies all the elements of Swaraj.

label: text
text: Mr. Das again condemned revolutionary violence, but said the co-operation invited by Lord Birkenhead is impossible in the present atmosphere of distrust. He declared that if the Swaraj's settlement was not responded to they must continue to make administration impossible and be prepared for ultimate civil disobedience; but he did not anticipate such a contingency, as he saw signs of reconciliation everywhere.
